S E C T I O N 2 · C R O S S - C U T T I N G I M P A C T
Climate Impacts Across Sectors
Every major sector of the economy faces distinct, material climate risk.
Agriculture
Shifting rainfall, heat stress, and pest ranges 
threaten yields and farmer livelihoods 
worldwide.
Water Resources
Glacial melt and erratic monsoons strain 
freshwater supply for drinking, farming, and 
industry.
Public Health
Heat-related illness, vector-borne disease, 
and air pollution impose rising healthcare 
burdens.
Infrastructure
Roads, power grids, and buildings face stress 
from floods, heat, and extreme weather 
events.
Energy
Both energy demand (cooling) and supply 
(hydro, thermal plant cooling water) are 
climate-sensitive.
Tourism & Aviation
Coastal and snow tourism destinations face 
existential risk; aviation faces both impact 
and mitigation pressure.
Insurance & Finance
Rising climate losses are repricing risk across 
insurance, banking, and real estate markets.
Digital Infrastructure
Data centers need constant cooling and 
power — both increasingly climate￾constrained resources.

S E C T I O N 2 · S P O T L I G H T F O R Y O U
Climate Change Meets Digital Infrastructure
This is the sector you are entering. It is not exempt — it is deeply exposed.
Data Center Cooling Data centers already consume ~1–1.5% of global electricity, with cooling as a major share. Rising ambient 
temperatures increase cooling costs and strain reliability.
Water Stress Many hyperscale data centers use water-based cooling. Regions facing water scarcity are increasingly restricting 
or taxing data center water use.
Grid Reliability Extreme weather increasingly threatens power grid stability — exactly the infrastructure cloud services depend 
on for uptime.
The Flip Side The same sector causing part of the problem is also building the tools — AI, IoT, digital twins — used to solve it. 
That tension is now central to the profession you are entering.

S E C T I O N 3 O F 4
Responses & Mitigation
Two strategies, many actors — from national governments to individual choices.
16

S E C T I O N 3 · T W O C O R E S T R A T E G I E S
Mitigation vs. Adaptation
Mitigation Adaptation
Reducing or preventing greenhouse gas emissions at the source. Adjusting systems and behavior to cope with climate impacts already 
happening.
Example: switching a power grid from coal to solar and wind. Example: building sea walls or flood-resistant infrastructure.
Example: improving energy efficiency in buildings and industry. Example: developing drought-resistant crop varieties.
Goal: address the root cause — slow or stop future warming. Goal: manage the consequences — reduce harm from current and locked-in 
warming.
Needed because: some warming is still avoidable. Needed because: some warming is already locked in, regardless of mitigation.

S E C T I O N 3 · S T A T E A G E N C I E S
How Governments & International Bodies Respond
National and international institutions set the frameworks within which everyone else operates.
International Bodies The UNFCCC coordinates global negotiations; the IPCC provides the scientific assessments that inform them.
National Governments Set emissions targets (NDCs), carbon pricing policies, renewable energy mandates, and building codes.
India's Response The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) coordinates 8 national missions spanning solar energy, 
energy efficiency, water, and sustainable habitats.
Sub-National Action States, cities, and municipalities increasingly set their own targets — often faster-moving than national policy.
CLI MAT E & SUST AI N AB I LI T Y · CON CE R N S, I MP ACT S, R E SP ON SE S & P R OT OCOLS 18

S E C T I O N 3 · N O N - S T A T E A G E N C I E S
How Industry & Civil Society Respond
Governments do not act alone — markets, institutions, and individuals all shape outcomes.
Private Sector Corporations set net-zero targets, invest in renewable energy, and face growing pressure from investors on 
climate risk (ESG).
NGOs & Civil Society Organizations like WWF, Greenpeace, and thousands of local groups drive advocacy, research, and on-ground 
conservation.
Academia & Research Universities and research institutions generate the science, models, and technologies mitigation and adaptation 
depend on.
Individuals & Communities Consumption choices, voting behavior, and grassroots organizing shape both markets and policy from the 
bottom up.

S E C T I O N 3 · Y O U R A N G L E
Climate Tech: Where Mitigation Meets Code
A fast-growing, talent-starved segment of the tech industry — and most CS graduates aren't looking at it yet.
Grid & Energy Software AI-driven platforms like Tesla Autobidder trade and dispatch battery power across grids in real time.
Carbon Accounting Platforms Startups like Watershed and Persefoni use data pipelines to automate enterprise emissions reporting — a 
booming SaaS category.
Climate Risk Analytics Financial institutions increasingly need software to model and price physical and transition climate risk.
The Career Signal Climate-tech hiring has grown faster than general tech hiring in recent years, while remaining comparatively 
under-supplied with engineering talent.

Climate Protocols & Agreements
The evolving legal and diplomatic architecture behind global climate action.

S E C T I O N 4 · T H E D I P L O M A T I C T I M E L I N E
Major Climate Agreements, 1972–Present
1972
Stockholm Conference — the first major UN 
conference on the human environment.
1992
UNFCCC adopted at the Rio Earth Summit —
the founding treaty for climate negotiations.
1997
Kyoto Protocol — the first treaty with binding 
emissions targets, for developed nations.
2015
Paris Agreement — nearly universal, 
nationally-determined climate commitments.
2021
COP26, Glasgow — India announces its 
"Panchamrit" five-point climate pledge.
2023+
COP28 & beyond — the first "Global 
Stocktake" of collective progress against the 
Paris Agreement.

S E C T I O N 4 · D E E P D I V E
The Paris Agreement — Key Features
Adopted in 2015 by 196 parties, the Paris Agreement remains the central framework for global climate action.
The Core Goal Limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) Each country sets its own emissions targets, reviewed and strengthened every five years.
Global Stocktake A periodic review of collective progress toward the Agreement's goals, informing the next round of NDCs.
Climate Finance Developed nations committed to mobilizing climate finance to support developing nations' mitigation and 
adaptation.

S E C T I O N 4 · Y O U R A N G L E
Why Every Protocol Needs an MRV System
A climate agreement is only as credible as the data behind it — and that data has to come from somewhere.
The MRV Problem Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) is how the world checks whether countries and companies are 
actually meeting their climate pledges.
Satellite Verification Independent satellite monitoring (e.g. methane-tracking missions) increasingly cross-checks self-reported 
national and corporate emissions data.
Blockchain & Carbon Markets Emerging carbon-credit registries use distributed ledgers to reduce double-counting and fraud in voluntary 
carbon markets.
The Opportunity Every treaty in this timeline ultimately depends on trustworthy software systems to prove it is actually working 
— that dependency is only growing.

◆ INTERACTIVE M A T C H T H E P R O T O C O L
Which climate agreement first introduced legally binding emissions 
targets — but only for developed nations?
A The Stockholm Declaration (1972)
B The UNFCCC (1992)
C The Kyoto Protocol (1997)
D The Paris Agreement (2015)
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. The Kyoto Protocol (1997)
The Kyoto Protocol was the first treaty to set binding 
emissions reduction targets, but only for industrialized 
("Annex I") countries. The Paris Agreement later 
moved to a more universal, nationally-determined 
model covering nearly all countries.

S E S S I O N R E C A P
From Concern to Commitment
1
Global Concerns
Sea level rise, extreme weather, biodiversity loss, food & water security, and migration 
— already unfolding, not future risks.
2
A Data Problem Too
Every global concern depends on monitoring, early-warning, and modeling systems to 
be managed at all.
3
Sectoral Impacts
From agriculture to digital infrastructure — no sector, including yours, is untouched.
4
Your Sector, Exposed
Data centers face real cooling, water, and grid-reliability risk from the very crisis their 
tools help solve.
5
Mitigation vs. Adaptation
Reducing emissions at the source, versus managing the impacts already locked in —
both are necessary.
6
State & Non-State Actors
Governments set frameworks; companies, NGOs, academia, and individuals all shape 
outcomes within them.
7
Climate Tech Careers
Grid software, carbon accounting, and climate risk analytics are fast-growing, talent￾starved fields.
8
The Protocol Timeline
From Stockholm (1972) through Kyoto (1997) to Paris (2015) — an evolving architecture 
for collective action.
9
India's Panchamrit
500 GW non-fossil capacity, 50% renewables, and net-zero by 2070 — ambition 
balanced against development needs.
10 MRV Needs Engineers
Every treaty depends on trustworthy data systems to prove commitments are actually 
being met.
